key_insight: Large language models can nearly match experts and outperform laypeople when rating empathic communication — provided the evaluation criteria are clear and specific.
problem_solved: Human evaluation of empathy is costly, variable, and slow; the paper evaluates whether LLMs can provide reliable, scalable judgments comparable to expert raters.
method: Systematic comparison of ratings from LLMs, domain experts, and lay raters across multiple established empathic-communication frameworks.
Quantified agreement and reliability (e.g., inter-rater metrics) to benchmark LLM performance against humans.
Tested the effect of rubric/prompt clarity and specificity on rater reliability to identify conditions where LLMs excel.
impact: Shows LLMs can be a scalable, cost-effective alternative for reliable empathy assessment in research and product workflows — but only when paired with clear evaluation rubrics, informing better human-AI evaluation design.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing inter-rater reliability scores for LLMs, experts, and lay raters across frameworks
Flowchart of the evaluation pipeline: inputs (dialogs) → rubric/prompt → rater type → scoring → agreement analysis
Before/after examples illustrating how rubric specificity improves LLM and human agreement (side-by-side text + scores)
Heatmap showing LLM performance variability across different empathy frameworks and rubric granularities
paper_title: When large language models are reliable for judging empathic communication
paper_authors: Aakriti Kumar, Nalin Poungpeth, Diyi Yang, Erina Farrell, Bruce L. Lambert
